title: Lecture 17. Action Plan of the Preventive Program
summary:
=== 17. Prevention Program Action Plan ===

1 Classification of Prevention Methods

2 Selection of Prevention Methods

1. Classification of Prevention Methods In the session dedicated to discussing prevention models, we have already discussed the structure of prevention stages and target groups. Below is a classification of the main prevention methods, correlated with its stages and target groups.

Prevention Stages Prevention Target Groups Prevention Methods
PRIMARY PREVENTION  

Universal prevention (universal)

    The entire population or youth subpopulation, territorial level     Legislative measures (e.g., tobacco advertising ban), social norms, and public initiatives. Information aimed at motivating «healthy» behavior and minimizing risk behavior, through traditional and internet mass media, visual and mobile printed materials, mass events (holidays, competitions, station games, theatrical performances, etc.) Integration into the school curriculum: development of life skills (life skills), emotional intelligence development, safe behavior in life and online, etc. Programs for developing psychological literacy among students, their parents, and educators
Selective prevention (selective) Risk groups, with a generally high level of stress Minimizing NON-specific risk factors through:
  • early identification of individuals in risk groups;
  • group work: discussions, debates, psychological trainings, and group consultations (e.g., stress management trainings for students before exams, support groups for young people experiencing parental divorce, discussion clubs for teenagers on health issues, relationship building, violence prevention, etc.).
  • network influence (involving target group members themselves, individuals with highly similar characteristics, or opinion leaders in disseminating prevention messages): «peer-to-peer« programs, parent clubs;
  • individual work: psychological counseling and psychotherapy.
Remote psychological support (helplines, bots, etc.)
Indicative prevention (indicated) Representatives of any risk groups, with specific signs of any behavioral disorder Individual prevention work (long-term interdisciplinary), aimed at minimizing specific risk factors:
  • identification of individuals in risk groups (observation in life and online, tests, diagnostic interviews, etc.);
  • network influence, for example, a «peer-to-peer« program among adolescents, where trained peer volunteers conduct information sessions and counseling on drug addiction prevention, violence, STIs, HIV, suicidal behavior, etc.;
  • psychological support: individual, group, family;
  • pedagogical support: assistance in organizing the educational process and developing an individual educational plan for a child with learning difficulties, employment and career planning, assistance in organizing leisure activities;
  • social case management, outcome monitoring (case management): social readaptation, assistance in obtaining medical services, assistance in employment, legal support, etc. within the law enforcement and judicial system, assistance in obtaining and restoring documents, etc.
SECONDARY PREVENTION Individuals with a diagnosis or pronounced signs of behavioral, social, or legal norm violations Minimizing negative consequences and preventing relapses through: Emergency psychological assistance. Training educational organization staff on action algorithms in case of emergencies. Medical, including narcological, psychiatric, and psychotherapeutic assistance. Outreach work (from English. Out of Reach – inaccessible): staff of prevention projects themselves go to places where hard-to-reach risk groups are concentrated (street children, individuals involved in prostitution, homeless people, drug users, etc.) and provide relevant and accessible preventive interventions. Social and legal support for detained adolescents, carried out (usually) by NGO services in conjunction with the law enforcement system. Assistance from social workers in restoring social connections and solving everyday problems for individuals in places of deprivation of liberty
TERTIARY PREVENTION Individuals after treatment or overcoming the acute phase of any excesses Rehabilitation, resocialization, and prevention of disability after an illness or crisis. Physical and psychological rehabilitation after recovery or overcoming the acute stage of illness. Social readaptation. Work with the social environment: family, educational team, etc. Long-term support, working with the environment Self-help groups

2. Selection of Prevention Methods The selection of prevention methods for the program is carried out in accordance with the following principles and recommendations.

  • Each task of the prevention program must be supported by an appropriate method or several methods. Conversely, all methods must stem from the program's objectives; the program should not contain work methods that lack justification and purpose.
  • Correspondence to the level of intervention. If the program was conceived at the level of universal prevention, strong additional justifications are required for conducting training sessions in small groups. Conversely, if we are talking about indicative prevention, mass media campaigns are also a non-priority method, with rare exceptions.

How to do it: For universal prevention of alcohol consumption among adolescents, it is effective to conduct school-wide information campaigns, interactive sessions to develop critical thinking regarding alcohol advertising, and organize sports events as an alternative to substance use. How not to do it: Conducting individual consultations with each student on alcohol consumption within a universal prevention program is inefficient in terms of resources and does not correspond to the level of intervention.

  • Correspondence to the planned subject of intervention (e.g., awareness, attitudes, behavior). It should be noted that methods that do not involve real interaction with the target audience (e.g., traditional lectures and mass media campaigns) can be successful in changing cognitive and emotional components of attitudes, but are extremely rarely effective in forming new behavior patterns and changing individual-personal characteristics and interpersonal relationship features. However, since the overall goal of prevention is behavior change, priority should be given to active methods, primarily those aimed at forming new skills.

How to do it: To develop skills for refusing drug offers, it is effective to use role-playing games, self-confidence trainings, and group discussions where participants can practice various scenarios and behavioral strategies. How not to do it: Limiting oneself to a lecture on the dangers of drugs – this may increase awareness, but is unlikely to lead to the formation of stable refusal skills.

  • Intervention complexity. Methods should support each other's mutual influence; for example, acquiring new skills can be combined with changing the psychological climate within a team and organization.

How to do it: A school bullying prevention program can include information sessions for all students, training for educators on methods of responding to bullying, the creation of a school mediation service, and the development and implementation of a school code of conduct. How not to do it: Focusing only on punishing aggressors without working with victims, witnesses, and the school environment as a whole.

  • Intensity of prevention. The more complex the behavior (or attitude) we want to change, the more intensive the program should be. In this case, intensity refers to both the overall duration of the program and the frequency of contact sessions, their duration, breaks between them, and their quality.

How to do it: To change deeply ingrained destructive behavior patterns (e.g., in addictions), a long-term program with regular and intensive psychotherapy sessions, group work, and social support is necessary. How not to do it: A single informational lecture is unlikely to lead to significant changes in such complex behavior.

  • Qualification of personnel implementing the intervention. Insufficient staff qualifications can lead to a lack of any effect or even a negative effect, even with the most correctly chosen methods.
  • Correspondence to project resources. A small pilot, but high-quality and effective project will have greater value than a methodologically underdeveloped or under-resourced project, even if it has a high coverage of the target group.
